Behavioral Patterns

Behavioral design patterns are concerned with algorithms and the assignment of responsibilities between objects.

They do not merely describe patterns of objects or classes, but also the patterns of communication between them. By using behavioral patterns, you can decouple senders from receivers, encapsulate stateful transitions, and structure complex control flows that would otherwise be difficult to trace and maintain.

The canonical Gang of Four (GoF) behavioral patterns include:

  1. Strategy
  2. Observer
  3. Command
  4. Chain of Responsibility
  5. State
  6. Template Method
  7. Iterator
  8. Mediator
  9. Memento
  10. Visitor

1. Strategy Pattern

The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one inside a dedicated class, and makes them interchangeable at runtime. It lets the algorithm vary independently from the clients that use it.

Technical Invariants

  1. Open-Closed Principle (OCP): New algorithms can be introduced without modifying existing client code or conditional statements.
  2. Elimination of Conditional Branches: Eliminates massive if/else or switch blocks that select algorithms based on runtime flags.
  3. First-Class Modern Idiom: In modern languages supporting first-class functions (Java 8+ lambdas, Python, TypeScript, Go), strategies can simply be passed as function references without creating separate classes.
// Strategy Interface
@FunctionalInterface
public interface PricingStrategy {
    BigDecimal calculate(BigDecimal basePrice);
}

// Context
public class ShoppingCart {
    private final List<BigDecimal> items = new ArrayList<>();
    private PricingStrategy pricingStrategy;

    public ShoppingCart(PricingStrategy pricingStrategy) {
        this.pricingStrategy = pricingStrategy;
    }

    public void setPricingStrategy(PricingStrategy strategy) {
        this.pricingStrategy = strategy;
    }

    public void addItem(BigDecimal price) { items.add(price); }

    public BigDecimal checkoutTotal() {
        BigDecimal subtotal = items.stream().reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
        return pricingStrategy.calculate(subtotal);
    }
}

// Client Usage with Lambdas or Dedicated Strategies:
ShoppingCart cart = new ShoppingCart(subtotal -> subtotal.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.90))); // 10% discount

Real-World Occurrences

  • Comparator.comparing(...) in Java collections sorting.
  • Payment processing engines switching between Stripe, PayPal, and Adyen strategies.

2. Observer Pattern

The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.

It is the foundation of event-driven architectures, pub/sub messaging, and modern reactive frameworks.

Technical Invariants

  1. Loose Coupling: The Subject knows only that its observers implement the Observer interface; it maintains no knowledge of their concrete classes or downstream behaviors.
  2. Broadcast Notification: The Subject iterates through an internal collection of registered observers and pushes (or signals) state changes without expecting return values.
  3. Dynamic Subscription: Observers can subscribe or unsubscribe at runtime.
// Observer interface
public interface OrderEventListener {
    void onOrderPlaced(String orderId, BigDecimal amount);
}

// Subject
public class OrderService {
    private final List<OrderEventListener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    public void subscribe(OrderEventListener listener) { listeners.add(listener); }
    public void unsubscribe(OrderEventListener listener) { listeners.remove(listener); }

    public void placeOrder(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        // Business logic
        System.out.println("Order " + orderId + " persisted to database.");

        // Broadcast event to observers
        for (OrderEventListener listener : listeners) {
            listener.onOrderPlaced(orderId, amount);
        }
    }
}

// Observers
public class EmailNotificationService implements OrderEventListener {
    @Override
    public void onOrderPlaced(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        System.out.println("Sending confirmation email for order: " + orderId);
    }
}

public class InventorySyncService implements OrderEventListener {
    @Override
    public void onOrderPlaced(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        System.out.println("Deducting warehouse stock for order: " + orderId);
    }
}

Real-World Occurrences

  • Spring Framework: ApplicationEventPublisher and @EventListener.
  • Reactive Streams: RxJava, Project Reactor (Flux / Mono), RxJS.

3. Command Pattern

The Command pattern converts a request or action into a stand-alone object containing all the information needed to execute, queue, log, or undo that operation. By packaging the intent and its parameters into an independent object, the caller (Invoker) is completely decoupled from the object that actually performs the work (Receiver).

Core Components

[ Client ] ─── creates ───► [ ConcreteCommand ] ─── invokes ───► [ Receiver ]
                                    │
                               implements
                                    ▼
[ Invoker ] ───── calls ───► [ Command ]
  1. Command Interface: Declares an execution interface (typically execute() or run()).
  2. Concrete Command: Encapsulates the request parameters and delegates execution to the receiver.
  3. Receiver: The business logic or worker component that knows how to perform the actual operation.
  4. Invoker: Decides when to run the command (e.g., immediate execution, background thread, queue, or transactional pipeline).
  5. Client: Creates the command, sets its receiver, and hands it off to the invoker.

Real-World Production Architectures from GitHub

Example 1: Camunda BPM Engine (camunda/camunda-bpm-platform)

  • GitHub Repository: camunda/camunda-bpm-platform
  • Core Package: org.camunda.bpm.engine.impl.cmd

In Camunda, every single external API call (such as starting a process instance, claiming a task, or modifying variables) is encapsulated inside a Command<T>.

1. The Command Interface (Command.java)

Instead of directly interacting with databases and process states, Camunda models every engine operation as an implementation of Command<T>:

package org.camunda.bpm.engine.impl.interceptor;

public interface Command<T> {
    T execute(CommandContext commandContext);
}

Note that execute receives a CommandContext (the Receiver), giving the command access to transaction sessions, database persistence, and identity management.

2. The Concrete Command (StartProcessInstanceCmd)

When a user calls runtimeService.startProcessInstanceByKey("orderProcess"), Camunda instantiates a concrete command:

package org.camunda.bpm.engine.impl.cmd;

import org.camunda.bpm.engine.impl.interceptor.Command;
import org.camunda.bpm.engine.impl.interceptor.CommandContext;
import org.camunda.bpm.engine.runtime.ProcessInstance;

public class StartProcessInstanceCmd implements Command<ProcessInstance> {
    protected String processDefinitionKey;
    protected Map<String, Object> variables;

    public StartProcessInstanceCmd(String processDefinitionKey, Map<String, Object> variables) {
        this.processDefinitionKey = processDefinitionKey;
        this.variables = variables;
    }

    @Override
    public ProcessInstance execute(CommandContext commandContext) {
        // Obtains managers from CommandContext (Receiver)
        ProcessDefinitionManager processDefinitionManager = commandContext.getProcessDefinitionManager();
        ProcessDefinitionEntity definition = processDefinitionManager.findLatestProcessDefinitionByKey(processDefinitionKey);
        
        // Executes domain logic to instantiate the process
        ExecutionEntity processInstance = definition.createProcessInstance();
        processInstance.start(variables);
        return processInstance;
    }
}
3. The Invoker & Interceptor Pipeline (CommandExecutor)

Execution is handled by a CommandExecutor that runs the command through a chain of interceptors (Logging, Security, and Transaction Context):

public interface CommandExecutor {
    <T> T execute(Command<T> command);
}

// In client code / Public Service Facade:
public class RuntimeServiceImpl implements RuntimeService {
    protected CommandExecutor commandExecutor;

    @Override
    public ProcessInstance startProcessInstanceByKey(String processDefinitionKey, Map<String, Object> variables) {
        return commandExecutor.execute(new StartProcessInstanceCmd(processDefinitionKey, variables));
    }
}

Why Camunda Uses It:

  • Atomic Transactions: The interceptor chain wraps execute() inside a database transaction commit/rollback boundary.
  • Separation of Concerns: Public API methods (RuntimeService) don't need any database logic, transaction handling, or permission checks; they simply construct and dispatch commands.

Example 2: Netflix Hystrix (Netflix/Hystrix)

  • GitHub Repository: Netflix/Hystrix

Netflix Hystrix is a latency and fault-tolerance library designed to isolate points of access to remote systems and microservices. The entire core of Hystrix is built on the Command pattern.

1. The Command Base (HystrixCommand<R>)

Remote calls, latency-sensitive database queries, or third-party HTTP requests are wrapped inside subclasses of HystrixCommand<R>:

package com.netflix.hystrix;

public abstract class HystrixCommand<R> implements HystrixExecutable<R> {
    protected abstract R run() throws Exception;

    // Optional fallback if run() fails or times out
    protected R getFallback() {
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException("No fallback available.");
    }

    // Invoker methods
    public R execute() { ... }          // Synchronous
    public Future<R> queue() { ... }    // Asynchronous
    public Observable<R> toObservable() { ... } // Reactive stream
}
2. Concrete Command Implementation

A microservice developer defines a command with its specific parameters, timeouts, and fallback behavior:

public class FetchUserProfileCommand extends HystrixCommand<UserProfile> {
    private final UserRestClient restClient; // The Receiver
    private final String userId;

    public FetchUserProfileCommand(UserRestClient restClient, String userId) {
        super(Setter.withGroupKey(HystrixCommandGroupKey.Factory.asKey("UserServiceGroup"))
            .andCommandPropertiesDefaults(
                HystrixCommandProperties.Setter()
                    .withExecutionTimeoutInMilliseconds(800)
            ));
        this.restClient = restClient;
        this.userId = userId;
    }

    @Override
    protected UserProfile run() throws Exception {
        // Actual HTTP/RPC call to external service
        return restClient.getUserProfile(userId);
    }

    @Override
    protected UserProfile getFallback() {
        // Graceful degradation when the downstream service fails or times out
        return UserProfile.createGuestProfile(userId);
    }
}
3. Client Execution
// Synchronous execution:
UserProfile profile = new FetchUserProfileCommand(userRestClient, "usr_1029").execute();

// Asynchronous execution via thread pool:
Future<UserProfile> futureProfile = new FetchUserProfileCommand(userRestClient, "usr_1029").queue();

Why Netflix Uses It:

  • Thread & Semaphore Isolation (Bulkhead): Each command can be routed to a dedicated thread pool so downstream failures do not exhaust all server threads.
  • Circuit Breaker & Fallbacks: If commands repeatedly fail or time out, the circuit opens, bypassing run() and immediately calling getFallback().
  • Telemetry: Metrics (execution time, failure rate, concurrency limits) are monitored on a per-command basis.

Example 3: CLI Frameworks (remkop/picocli)

  • GitHub Repository: remkop/picocli

Command-line parsers like Picocli map CLI subcommands directly into standard Java Runnable or Callable<Integer> commands:

package com.example.cli;

import picocli.CommandLine;
import picocli.CommandLine.Command;
import picocli.CommandLine.Option;
import picocli.CommandLine.Parameters;
import java.io.File;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;

// Concrete Command
@Command(name = "encrypt", description = "Encrypts a file using AES-256")
public class EncryptCommand implements Callable<Integer> {

    @Parameters(index = "0", description = "The file to encrypt")
    private File file;

    @Option(names = {"-a", "--algorithm"}, defaultValue = "AES", description = "Cipher algorithm")
    private String algorithm;

    // The execute method
    @Override
    public Integer call() throws Exception {
        // Business logic interacting with the filesystem/crypto receiver
        CryptoEngine.encrypt(file, algorithm);
        System.out.println("Encrypted: " + file.getName());
        return 0; // Exit status
    }
}

// Invoker & Client
public class MainApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // CommandLine parses arguments, instantiates EncryptCommand, and invokes call()
        int exitCode = new CommandLine(new EncryptCommand()).execute(args);
        System.exit(exitCode);
    }
}

Deep Dive: The Resilience & Cascading Failure Problem

To understand why Netflix built Hystrix around the Command pattern, consider what happens to a standard production backend when dependencies degrade:

What Happens Without It: The Cascading Failure

In a typical web application (e.g., Tomcat with 200 worker threads), incoming HTTP requests are served using a shared thread pool:

Incoming Requests (User traffic)
        │
        ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               App Server Thread Pool                   │
│  [Thread 1]   -> Waiting on Recommendations (blocked)  │
│  [Thread 2]   -> Waiting on Recommendations (blocked)  │
│  [Thread 3]   -> Waiting on Recommendations (blocked)  │
│  ...                                                   │
│  [Thread 200] -> Waiting on Recommendations (blocked)  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
All worker threads exhausted!
Even critical paths (Login, Video playback) fail with 503/504.
  • Thread Pool Starvation: Because remote calls execute synchronously directly on the request thread, a single slow dependency holds threads hostage.
  • Cascading Failure: An optional, secondary feature (like "recommended movies") knocks out the entire application, preventing users from logging in or checking out.
  • Recovery Stampede: When the failing service tries to restart, thousands of queued requests instantly flood it, knocking it back down.

How the Command Pattern Solves This

  1. Bulkhead Isolation (Thread Pools / Semaphores): Instead of executing calls on the incoming web server threads, each HystrixCommand runs in its own bounded thread pool:
    • Catalog Pool: 15 threads max
    • Auth Pool: 20 threads max
    • Recommendations Pool: 10 threads max If Recommendations slows down, at most 10 threads block. The 11th request is rejected immediately without waiting. The main web server thread pool remains 100% free to serve logins and payments.
Incoming Request (Tomcat Thread)
        │
        ▼
[ FetchRecommendationsCmd ]
        │
        ├──► Routes to "Recommendations" Thread Pool (Cap: 10)
        │       └── All 10 threads full?
        │               └── Reject immediately!
        │
        └── Main web server thread never hangs.

  1. Fast Timeouts & Circuit Breaking: If a command exceeds a strict latency budget (e.g., 500 ms), Hystrix aborts waiting and triggers fallback logic. If failures surpass a threshold (e.g., >50% failure rate over 10 seconds), the Circuit Breaker trips OPEN:

    • All subsequent requests skip the network completely.
    • They fail-fast in 0 milliseconds and go straight to the fallback.
    • After a sleep window (e.g., 5 seconds), Hystrix lets a single probe request through ("half-open") to check recovery.

  2. Graceful Degradation (Fallback): Because the command object encapsulates the context and goal of the call, it can provide an alternative path:

public class GetRecommendationsCommand extends HystrixCommand<List<Movie>> {
    private final String userId;

    public GetRecommendationsCommand(String userId) {
        super(Setter.withGroupKey(HystrixCommandGroupKey.Factory.asKey("RecommendationGroup"))
            .andThreadPoolPropertiesDefaults(
                HystrixThreadPoolProperties.Setter()
                    .withCoreSize(10) // Bulkhead: max 10 threads
            )
            .andCommandPropertiesDefaults(
                HystrixCommandProperties.Setter()
                    .withExecutionTimeoutInMilliseconds(500) // Hard timeout
            ));
        this.userId = userId;
    }

    @Override
    protected List<Movie> run() throws Exception {
        // Degraded or hanging downstream service
        return recommendationClient.getPersonalized(userId);
    }

    @Override
    protected List<Movie> getFallback() {
        // Non-blocking fallback: serve cached static list of top 10 popular movies
        return StaticCache.getTopTenTrending();
    }
}

The user receives a complete page with trending movies rather than an error banner or an infinite loading spinner.

Side-by-Side Comparison

ScenarioWithout Command Pattern (Standard Call)With Hystrix Command Pattern
Downstream latency increases from 50ms to 30sCaller threads block and wait for 30s; container thread pool starves.Hystrix times out at 500ms, returns fallback, and frees caller thread.
Downstream service goes down completelyEvery request repeatedly burns sockets and CPU until total system failure.Circuit trips OPEN; subsequent requests bypass the network instantly in 0ms.
Non-essential service failsCan take down the entire system (e.g., comments outage breaks checkout).Bulkhead confines failure to its dedicated small pool; checkout continues unimpeded.
Recovery after an incidentThe recovering service is hit by a massive surge of pent-up traffic and crashes again.Circuit stays open and only lets small canary batches through until stability is verified.

[!NOTE] Modern Evolution: Resilience4j Netflix placed Hystrix into maintenance mode because its thread-per-command model carries context-switching overhead at extreme scale. Modern Java ecosystems use Resilience4j, which implements the exact same Command/Decorator patterns using lightweight functional interfaces (Supplier<T>, Runnable), atomic counters, and non-blocking asynchronous APIs (CompletableFuture, Project Reactor) without requiring dedicated thread pools for every dependency.

Why Not Just Use Node.js or Non-Blocking Runtimes?

Node.js avoids thread starvation because of its non-blocking event loop, but switching runtimes does not solve the underlying problem—it only shifts the catastrophic failure mode from thread exhaustion to memory exhaustion, socket saturation, and garbage collection freezes:

  1. V8 Heap Memory Exhaustion (OOM Crash): Every pending request in Node.js retains memory (active TCP socket buffers, Promise objects, closure headers, and tokens). At 500 req/sec with 30s latency, Node holds 15,000 unresolved promises in RAM, throwing: FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
  2. Socket Exhaustion (EMFILE): Once open sockets are tied up waiting on hanging responses, Node hits file descriptor limits (ulimit -n), rejecting new client connections with EMFILE: too many open files.
  3. Event Loop Lag & GC Freezes: Retaining tens of thousands of objects forces V8 into "Stop-the-World" Mark-Sweep garbage collection, halting the single JavaScript thread for hundreds of milliseconds and causing load balancers to mark the container dead.

In Node.js, libraries like Opossum or Cockatiel wrap asynchronous functions in the exact same Command-style circuit breaker abstraction:

import CircuitBreaker from 'opossum';

const options = {
    timeout: 500,                   // Trip if request takes longer than 500ms
    errorThresholdPercentage: 50,  // Open circuit if 50% of requests fail
    resetTimeout: 5000              // Test service health again after 5s
};

const breaker = new CircuitBreaker(fetchRecommendationsFromService, options);
breaker.fallback(() => getTrendingMoviesCache());

app.get('/recommendations/:userId', async (req, res) => {
    try {
        const data = await breaker.fire(req.params.userId);
        res.json(data);
    } catch (err) {
        res.status(500).json({ error: 'Service unavailable' });
    }
});

Thread-per-Request vs. Event-Driven Under Downstream Failure

Failure CharacteristicThreaded (Classic Java / Tomcat)Non-Blocking (Node.js / Netty / WebFlux)
Direct Impact of Slow I/OWorker threads sleep waiting for sockets; thread pool runs dry.Event loop stays free, but memory buffers and pending Promises accumulate.
Point of CollapseThread starvation (Requests rejected at container queue).V8 Heap Out of Memory (Process crash), or file descriptor exhaustion (EMFILE).
Impact on Other RoutesOther routes starve immediately because no worker thread is free.Fast routes continue until GC pressure freezes the event loop or memory crashes.
Remedy Without Circuit BreakerIncrease thread count (worsens context switching & memory).Increase RAM (postpones crash by a few seconds under sustained traffic).
Real SolutionCircuit breaker, hard timeouts, bounded bulkheads, fallbacks.Circuit breaker, hard timeouts, bounded concurrency, fallbacks.

End-to-End Production Example: API Call with Resilience

Here is a full end-to-end implementation tracing an incoming user request through the Command pattern—from REST controller to downstream execution, thread pool isolation (bulkhead), timeout handling, and fallback degradation:

[ Incoming HTTP Request: GET /api/movies/42/recommendations ]
                           │
                           ▼
               MovieController <── Client
                           │
               1. Instantiates Command
               2. Hands to Executor
                           │
                           ▼
            ResilientCommandExecutor <── Invoker
                           │
               Routes to dedicated thread pool (Bulkhead)
               Enforces hard timeout (e.g., 500ms)
                           │
                 ┌─────────┴─────────┐
            [ Success ]         [ Timeout / Error ]
                 │                   │
                 ▼                   ▼
       FetchRecommendationsCommand  FetchRecommendationsCommand
               .execute()                  .getFallback()
                 │                   │
                 ▼                   ▼
     RecommendationServiceClient    Static trending list / Cache
              (Receiver)
                 │                   │
                 └─────────┬─────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
          [ HTTP 200 OK: JSON Response returned ]

1. The Receiver (Performs Downstream HTTP Call)

The receiver knows how to talk to the remote service. It has zero knowledge of thread pools, circuit breakers, or controllers:

package com.example.receiver;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;
import java.util.List;

@Component
public class RecommendationServiceClient {
    private final RestClient restClient;

    public RecommendationServiceClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
        this.restClient = builder.baseUrl("https://recommendations.internal.service").build();
    }

    public List<String> fetchPersonalized(String movieId, String userId) {
        // Outbound HTTP call to downstream microservice
        return restClient.get()
                .uri("/v1/recommendations?movieId={movieId}&userId={userId}", movieId, userId)
                .retrieve()
                .body(List.class);
    }
}

2. The Command Abstraction & Concrete Command

The command encapsulates the receiver reference, request parameters, execution configuration, and fallback logic:

package com.example.command;

public interface ResilientCommand<T> {
    T execute() throws Exception;
    T getFallback(Throwable cause);
    String getGroupKey();       // Identifies which thread pool (bulkhead) to use
    long getTimeoutMillis();
}

package com.example.command;

import com.example.receiver.RecommendationServiceClient;
import java.util.List;

public class FetchRecommendationsCommand implements ResilientCommand<List<String>> {
    private final RecommendationServiceClient receiver;
    private final String movieId;
    private final String userId;

    public FetchRecommendationsCommand(RecommendationServiceClient receiver, String movieId, String userId) {
        this.receiver = receiver;
        this.movieId = movieId;
        this.userId = userId;
    }

    @Override
    public List<String> execute() {
        return receiver.fetchPersonalized(movieId, userId);
    }

    @Override
    public List<String> getFallback(Throwable cause) {
        System.err.println("Downstream call failed (" + cause.getMessage() + "). Serving fallback.");
        // Return static trending movies so the user still gets a complete page
        return List.of("Inception", "The Dark Knight", "Interstellar");
    }

    @Override
    public String getGroupKey() {
        return "recommendations-pool";
    }

    @Override
    public long getTimeoutMillis() {
        return 500; // Strict latency cap
    }
}

3. The Invoker (Bulkhead, Timeout, and Execution Engine)

The invoker maintains isolated thread pools for each dependency group, enforcing concurrency limits and timeouts:

package com.example.invoker;

import com.example.command.ResilientCommand;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

@Component
public class ResilientCommandExecutor {
    // Bulkhead: Dedicated thread pool with max 5 concurrent threads and a queue of 10
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, ExecutorService> threadPools = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    private ExecutorService getOrCreatePool(String groupKey) {
        return threadPools.computeIfAbsent(groupKey, key -> new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                5, 5, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10),              // Caps total backlog to prevent memory leaks
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()       // Reject immediately when saturated
        ));
    }

    public <T> CompletableFuture<T> executeAsync(ResilientCommand<T> command) {
        ExecutorService pool = getOrCreatePool(command.getGroupKey());
        try {
            return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
                try {
                    return command.execute();
                } catch (Exception e) {
                    throw new CompletionException(e);
                }
            }, pool)
            // Time out after the command's declared limit
            .orTimeout(command.getTimeoutMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            // If anything fails (timeout, rejected execution, 500 error), trigger fallback
            .exceptionally(command::getFallback);
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
            // Bulkhead is full: skip queueing and immediately execute fallback
            return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(command.getFallback(e));
        }
    }
}

4. The Client (Spring REST Controller)

package com.example.controller;

import com.example.command.FetchRecommendationsCommand;
import com.example.invoker.ResilientCommandExecutor;
import com.example.receiver.RecommendationServiceClient;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/movies")
public class MovieController {
    private final RecommendationServiceClient receiver;
    private final ResilientCommandExecutor invoker;

    public MovieController(RecommendationServiceClient receiver, ResilientCommandExecutor invoker) {
        this.receiver = receiver;
        this.invoker = invoker;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{movieId}/recommendations")
    public CompletableFuture<ResponseEntity<List<String>>> getRecommendations(
            @PathVariable String movieId,
            @RequestHeader(value = "X-User-Id", defaultValue = "guest") String userId) {
        // 1. Package the request into a Command object
        FetchRecommendationsCommand command = new FetchRecommendationsCommand(receiver, movieId, userId);

        // 2. Dispatch to the invoker
        return invoker.executeAsync(command)
                .thenApply(ResponseEntity::ok);
    }
}
Execution Walkthrough
  • Scenario A: Happy Path (Downstream responds in 40ms): Command runs on worker pool; returns ["Oppenheimer", "Tenet", "Memento"] in 40 ms. Tomcat request thread unbinds immediately.
  • Scenario B: Degraded Service (Downstream hangs for 20s): At 500 ms, .orTimeout() triggers TimeoutException. Fallback returns ["Inception", "The Dark Knight", "Interstellar"] in 502 ms total. Main server pool remains unblocked.
  • Scenario C: Downstream Outage Under High Load (100 concurrent requests): First 15 requests fill the 5 threads and 10-slot queue. Request 16 triggers RejectedExecutionException. Invoker immediately serves fallback in <1 ms without touching the network.

Classic Undoable Command Example (Editor History)

Commands can also retain prior state before execution to support multi-level .undo():

// Command interface with undo support
public interface UndoableCommand {
    void execute();
    void undo();
}

// Receiver
public class TextDocument {
    private final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();

    public void append(String str) { text.append(str); }
    public void deleteLast(int length) {
        int start = text.length() - length;
        text.delete(start, text.length());
    }
    public String getContent() { return text.toString(); }
}

// Concrete Command
public class InsertTextCommand implements UndoableCommand {
    private final TextDocument document;
    private final String textToInsert;

    public InsertTextCommand(TextDocument doc, String textToInsert) {
        this.document = doc;
        this.textToInsert = textToInsert;
    }

    @Override
    public void execute() {
        document.append(textToInsert);
    }

    @Override
    public void undo() {
        document.deleteLast(textToInsert.length());
    }
}

// Invoker: Command History Manager
public class EditorHistory {
    private final Deque<UndoableCommand> undoStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void executeCommand(UndoableCommand cmd) {
        cmd.execute();
        undoStack.push(cmd);
    }

    public void undo() {
        if (!undoStack.isEmpty()) {
            UndoableCommand cmd = undoStack.pop();
            cmd.undo();
        }
    }
}

When to Choose the Command Pattern

Use the Command pattern when an application needs:

  • Asynchronous & Deferred Execution: Placing operations in queues, message brokers, or scheduling thread pools (ExecutorService accepting Runnable/Callable).
  • Transactional Interception: Wrapping multiple disparate actions with consistent cross-cutting concerns (logging, audit trails, permission verification, transaction commits).
  • Undo/Redo Capabilities: Retaining a command history stack where each command pairs execute() with undo().
  • Fault Tolerance & Resilience: Wrapping network boundaries with bulkheads, timeouts, fallbacks, and circuit breakers.

Primary Trade-off: Class Proliferation—every discrete action requires its own class file and constructor boilerplate, which is unnecessary for simple, direct method calls within the same domain boundary.

4. Chain of Responsibility Pattern

The Chain of Responsibility is a behavioral design pattern that decouples the sender of a request from its receivers by organizing potential handlers into a pipeline, giving each handler the opportunity to process the request, mutate it, pass it down the line, or terminate the flow entirely.

While the classic Gang of Four (GoF) definition relies on each handler maintaining a direct reference to a successor (next.handle(request)), major Java open-source projects on GitHub typically implement the pattern using a centralized chain coordinator (passing a Chain context object) or an intrusive linked list of contexts. This avoids rigid handler coupling and prevents uncontrolled recursive stack growth.

Real-World Production Implementations from GitHub

Example 1: Jakarta Servlet API & Apache Tomcat (apache/tomcat)

  • GitHub Repository: apache/tomcat
  • Core Classes: jakarta.servlet.Filter, jakarta.servlet.FilterChain, org.apache.catalina.core.ApplicationFilterChain

The standard Java/Jakarta Servlet specification uses this pattern to preprocess HTTP requests (e.g., authentication, logging, compression, CORS) before reaching the target servlet.

Client Request
      │
      ▼
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         ApplicationFilterChain (Tomcat)       │
│                                               │
│  [pos = 0] Filter 1 (LoggingFilter)           │
│      │  chain.doFilter(...)                   │
│      ▼                                        │
│  [pos = 1] Filter 2 (AuthenticationFilter)    │
│      │  chain.doFilter(...)                   │
│      ▼                                        │
│  [pos = 2] Filter 3 (CorsFilter)              │
│      │  chain.doFilter(...)                   │
│      ▼                                        │
│  [pos == n] Target Servlet (service())        │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Production Source Code Pattern in Tomcat

Inside Tomcat's ApplicationFilterChain.java, the chain tracks its position in an internal array using an index counter:

// Simplified from org.apache.catalina.core.ApplicationFilterChain in apache/tomcat
public final class ApplicationFilterChain implements FilterChain {
    private ApplicationFilterConfig[] filters = new ApplicationFilterConfig[0];
    private int pos = 0; // Current position in the chain
    private int n = 0;   // Total number of filters
    private Servlet servlet;

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        internalDoFilter(request, response);
    }

    private void internalDoFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        // As long as there are filters left, advance and invoke the next one
        if (pos < n) {
            ApplicationFilterConfig filterConfig = filters[pos++];
            Filter filter = filterConfig.getFilter();
            // The filter gets 'this' (the chain) to trigger the next link
            filter.doFilter(request, response, this);
            return;
        }
        // End of the chain reached: invoke the ultimate destination
        servlet.service(request, response);
    }
}
Handler Implementation

Concrete handlers inspect or wrap the payload, then decide whether to proceed or short-circuit:

public class SecurityValidationFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletRequest request = (HttpServletRequest) req;
        HttpServletResponse response = (HttpServletResponse) res;

        String authHeader = request.getHeader("Authorization");
        if (authHeader == null || !authHeader.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
            // Short-circuit the chain: do not call chain.doFilter()
            response.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED, "Missing Token");
            return;
        }

        // Pass control to the next handler in the chain
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }
}

Example 2: Spring Security's FilterChainProxy (spring-projects/spring-security)

  • GitHub Repository: spring-projects/spring-security
  • Core Classes: org.springframework.security.web.FilterChainProxy, VirtualFilterChain

Spring Security injects a master servlet filter (FilterChainProxy) into the web container. When an HTTP request enters, FilterChainProxy delegates execution to a specialized chain of security-specific filters (such as CsrfFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, and AuthorizationFilter).

// Simplified from org.springframework.security.web.FilterChainProxy in spring-security
private static final class VirtualFilterChain implements FilterChain {
    private final FilterChain originalChain;
    private final List<Filter> additionalFilters;
    private final int size;
    private int currentPosition = 0;

    private VirtualFilterChain(FilterChain originalChain, List<Filter> additionalFilters) {
        this.originalChain = originalChain;
        this.additionalFilters = additionalFilters;
        this.size = additionalFilters.size();
    }

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        // If all Spring Security filters passed, proceed to the outer web container chain
        if (this.currentPosition == this.size) {
            this.originalChain.doFilter(request, response);
            return;
        }
        this.currentPosition++;
        Filter nextFilter = this.additionalFilters.get(this.currentPosition - 1);
        // Execute the filter, passing 'this' virtual chain
        nextFilter.doFilter(request, response, this);
    }
}

This ensures that if CsrfFilter rejects a token, it writes an error response and halts the chain. Subsequent filters (like password authentication or endpoint authorization) are never invoked.

Example 3: Netty ChannelPipeline (netty/netty)

  • GitHub Repository: netty/netty
  • Core Classes: io.netty.channel.ChannelPipeline, io.netty.channel.ChannelInboundHandler, io.netty.channel.DefaultChannelPipeline

Netty handles high-throughput asynchronous networking. Each network socket (Channel) has a ChannelPipeline implementing a two-way Chain of Responsibility:

  • Inbound events (bytes received from network) move forward through the chain (Head $\rightarrow$ Tail).
  • Outbound events (bytes being sent to network) move backward through the chain (Tail $\rightarrow$ Head).
  HeadContext                                            TailContext
┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│   ChannelRead    │ ───► │  ByteToMessage   │ ───► │ BusinessHandler  │
│ (Inbound Start)  │      │    (Decoder)     │      │ (Process Logic)  │
└──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘
         ▲                         │                         │
         │                         ▼                         ▼
┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│   Write/Flush    │ ◄─── │  MessageToByte   │ ◄─── │  Response Data   │
│ (Outbound Exit)  │      │    (Encoder)     │      │ (Outbound Start) │
└──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘
Production Source Code Pattern in Netty

Instead of an index counter, Netty uses a doubly-linked list of context nodes (AbstractChannelHandlerContext):

// Simplified snippet from io.netty.channel.AbstractChannelHandlerContext in netty/netty
abstract class AbstractChannelHandlerContext implements ChannelHandlerContext {
    volatile AbstractChannelHandlerContext next;
    volatile AbstractChannelHandlerContext prev;

    @Override
    public ChannelHandlerContext fireChannelRead(final Object msg) {
        // Locate the next inbound handler node in the doubly linked list
        AbstractChannelHandlerContext next = findContextInbound(MASK_CHANNEL_READ);
        next.invokeChannelRead(msg);
        return this;
    }

    private void invokeChannelRead(Object msg) {
        try {
            ((ChannelInboundHandler) handler()).channelRead(this, msg);
        } catch (Throwable t) {
            notifyHandlerException(t);
        }
    }
}
Handler Implementation

Handlers decide what data types to consume, transform, or re-emit to the next link:

public class FrameDecoder extends ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter {
    @Override
    public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) {
        ByteBuf in = (ByteBuf) msg;
        if (in.readableBytes() >= 4) {
            int length = in.readInt();
            ByteBuf frame = in.readRetainedSlice(length);
            // Forward the decoded frame to the next handler in the pipeline
            ctx.fireChannelRead(frame);
        } else {
            // Buffer does not have enough bytes yet; wait for more data without propagating
            in.discardReadBytes();
        }
    }
}

Comparison of Real-World Implementations

ProjectChain TopologyExecution ModelTermination Strategy
Apache TomcatDynamic array (Filter[]) with index pointerOnion/Wrapper: Pre-processing $\rightarrow$ doFilter() $\rightarrow$ Post-processing on unwindOmit calling chain.doFilter() to return response immediately
Spring SecurityList<Filter> wrapped in VirtualFilterChainSequential validation: Verifies tokens, session context, and authorization checksSend HTTP error status (401/403) and omit calling chain.doFilter()
NettyDoubly-linked list (HeadContext <-> TailContext)Bidirectional: Inbound data flows forward; outbound data flows backwardOmit calling ctx.fireChannelRead(msg) or release buffer

GoF vs. Production Implementations

  1. Decoupling the Handler from its Successor: GoF defines Handler.setNext(Handler next). In enterprise engines like Spring or Tomcat, handlers never hold references to one another. They interact solely with a shared FilterChain or ChannelHandlerContext, allowing frameworks to insert, reorder, or remove links dynamically at runtime without rebuilding individual handler objects.
  2. Two-Way Processing ("Around" Advice): Real-world implementations frequently need "around" advice (executing code before and after the downstream handlers). The chain.doFilter(req, res) paradigm allows code after the call to intercept responses during the unwinding phase of the stack.

Why Recursive Delegation (chain.doFilter()) Instead of a For Loop?

The recursive delegation pattern—where the chain calls the handler, and the handler calls the chain back—is used instead of a for loop primarily to enable the "Onion" (Around) model: handlers can execute code both before and after downstream components run.

A simple for loop only works for unidirectional, flat processing. It falls apart as soon as handlers need post-processing, response wrapping, resource cleanup, or asynchronous delegation.

1. Two-Way Execution ("Around Advice")

Many handlers must sandwich the rest of the application between setup and teardown logic. The call stack maintains this ordering automatically:

[Request Inbound]
      │
      ▼
LoggingFilter: Start timer
      │ chain.doFilter()
      ▼
AuthenticationFilter: Authenticate user
      │ chain.doFilter()
      ▼
Target Servlet: Process business logic
      ▲
      │ Stack unwinds (returns)
AuthenticationFilter: Commit session
      ▲
      │ Stack unwinds (returns)
LoggingFilter: Stop timer & log total duration
      │
      ▼
[Response Outbound]

public class LatencyMetricsFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();

        // 1. Pre-processing: pass control down the rest of the chain
        chain.doFilter(req, res);

        // 2. Post-processing: runs after the Servlet AND all inner filters finish
        long duration = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;
        System.out.println("Downstream processing took: " + duration + " ms");
    }
}

Why a for loop fails here: In a for (Filter f : filters) loop, once f.execute(req) returns, that filter's stack frame is gone. To achieve the same behavior in a loop, you would need to split every handler into two distinct methods (preHandle and postHandle) and run two separate loops across an inverted stack or list.

2. Request and Response Wrapping (Decorator Pattern)

In servlet architectures, filters often alter how downstream components write or read data—such as compressing output with GZIP, encrypting payloads, or caching response streams. They achieve this by wrapping HttpServletResponse in an HttpServletResponseWrapper:

public class GzipFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        // Wrap the response with a GZIP-compressing stream
        GzipResponseWrapper wrappedResponse = new GzipResponseWrapper((HttpServletResponse) res);

        // Pass the WRAPPER down the chain; downstream writes directly into this wrapper
        chain.doFilter(req, wrappedResponse);

        // After downstream writes are finished, finalize and compress the buffer
        wrappedResponse.finishCompression();
    }
}

Because chain.doFilter() accepts the modified parameter, scope is tightly bound to that specific invocation. When execution returns up to this filter, it can flush the compressed stream directly back to the physical client socket.

3. Native Exception Handling and Resource Cleanup

A recursive stack allows handlers to wrap the execution of the entire downstream application in standard Java try-catch-finally blocks:

public class SecurityContextCleanupFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        try {
            SecurityContextHolder.setContext(authenticatedContext);
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } catch (AccessDeniedException ex) {
            // Intercept downstream exceptions and turn them into 403 responses
            ((HttpServletResponse) res).sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN);
        } finally {
            // Guaranteed cleanup of ThreadLocal variables to avoid memory leaks in thread pools
            SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();
        }
    }
}

4. Non-Blocking / Asynchronous Pipelines (e.g., Netty)

A for loop forces synchronous, single-threaded execution. In event-driven frameworks like Netty, a handler can execute an asynchronous task before allowing the request to continue:

public class AsyncAuthHandler extends ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter {
    @Override
    public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) {
        authClient.validateTokenAsync(msg).addListener(future -> {
            if (future.isSuccess()) {
                // Asynchronously resume the chain whenever the background task finishes,
                // potentially on an entirely different worker thread
                ctx.fireChannelRead(msg);
            } else {
                ctx.close();
            }
        });
    }
}

Summary: When to Use Which

RequirementRecursive Delegation (chain.doFilter())Flat Iteration (for loop)
Execution Flow"Around" (before + after execution)"Before only" (unidirectional)
Payload MutationCan substitute/wrap request or response for downstream componentsHandlers modify state within shared mutable objects
Error HandlingNatural try-catch-finally enclosing downstream logicRequires error state flags or centralized catch blocks
Async / ReactiveHandlers can defer calling next until a Future/callback completesThread-blocking; cannot suspend mid-loop
Stack DepthConsumes stack frames proportional to chain lengthConstant stack memory ($O(1)$)

Does This Create Stack Creep / Excessive Recursion?

It absolutely creates stack creep—which is why anyone who has ever debugged a Spring Boot application is familiar with the 80-line "wall of text" stack trace dominated by alternating lines of FilterChainProxy.doFilter() and ApplicationFilterChain.internalDoFilter().

However, the architecture accepts this trade-off because web and application filters operate well inside safe JVM memory thresholds:

The Reality of Stack Memory

In a 64-bit HotSpot JVM, the default thread stack size (-Xss) is 1,024 KB (1 MB). A typical Java stack frame for a filter invocation carries only:

  • The return address
  • A couple of object references (HttpServletRequest, HttpServletResponse, FilterChain)
  • Local variables and the operand stack

This averages roughly 32 to 128 bytes per frame.

Total Stack Allocation (-Xss1024k)
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Filter Chain (~30 filters × 2 frames = 60 frames) ≈ 8 KB  │ < 1% of stack
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Controller / Service / Repository calls ≈ 20-40 KB        │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Remaining Headroom for Business Logic ≈ 970 KB            │ > 95% free
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A standard Spring Boot enterprise application rarely exceeds 15 to 30 filters. Because each link in the chain adds 2 stack frames (chain.doFilter() calling filter.doFilter()), the pipeline consumes about 30 to 60 frames—amounting to roughly 5 to 10 KB of stack memory, or less than 1% of the thread's stack limit.

Because the length of these infrastructure chains is statically bounded by application configuration, the risk of a true StackOverflowError is virtually zero.

The Real Costs of Stack Creep

  • Stack Trace Pollution ("The Scroll of Death"): When a database call fails, finding the root application error requires scrolling past screens of infrastructure boilerplate.
  • Debugging Fatigue: Stepping through code with an IDE debugger forces you to step in and out of the chain coordinator at every single link.
  • No JVM Tail-Call Optimization (TCO): Standard JVM bytecode (invokevirtual) does not support automatic tail-call elimination; every call allocates a physical frame.

Where It Becomes Fatal: Unbounded Chains

When a chain does not have 20 steps, but thousands (such as a rules engine evaluating 5,000 validation rules or an AST traversal), recursive delegation will blow up the stack. In those scenarios, production systems use two alternative designs:

1. The Trampoline / Event Loop (The "Work-Queue Drain" Pattern)

Frameworks like Netty, RxJava, and Project Reactor use a drain loop on the heap:

public class NonRecursivePipeline {
    private final Queue<Runnable> taskQueue = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
    private final AtomicInteger wip = new AtomicInteger(); // Work In Progress counter

    public void submit(Runnable task) {
        taskQueue.offer(task);
        drain();
    }

    private void drain() {
        // If wip > 0, another thread or frame is already draining the queue.
        // Return immediately to flatten the call stack!
        if (wip.getAndIncrement() == 0) {
            do {
                Runnable task = taskQueue.poll();
                if (task != null) {
                    task.run(); // Flat call: returns immediately, stack depth = 1
                }
            } while (wip.decrementAndGet() > 0);
        }
    }
}
2. Explicit Stack / State Machine

If a framework needs the "Around" behavior for thousands of links without stack recursion, it moves the call stack from the OS thread stack to an in-memory Java collection on the heap:

public class FlatAroundChain {
    private final List<Interceptor> interceptors;

    public void execute(Context ctx) {
        Deque<Interceptor> executed = new ArrayDeque<>();

        // 1. Pre-processing: flat loop forward
        for (Interceptor interceptor : interceptors) {
            boolean proceed = interceptor.before(ctx);
            executed.push(interceptor);
            if (!proceed) break; // Short-circuit
        }

        // 2. Core action
        ctx.dispatch();

        // 3. Post-processing: flat loop backward (unwinding the stack manually)
        while (!executed.isEmpty()) {
            Interceptor interceptor = executed.pop();
            interceptor.after(ctx);
        }
    }
}

Architectural Evolution in Modern Web Frameworks

Modern web frameworks have mostly moved away from deep, synchronous, call-stack recursion:

Era / Framework StyleTypical FrameworksPrimary MechanismHow Stack Growth Is Managed
Classic SynchronousSpring MVC, Jakarta Servlets, Apache TomcatDirect mutual recursion (chain.doFilter)Stack frames are kept tiny; chains are limited to $N \le 50$ so 1 MB -Xss is never exceeded.
Async / Promise ChainsKoa, Fastify, Express 5+Promises / Microtasks (async/await, koa-compose)Handlers suspend at I/O boundaries; call context lives in heap microtasks, not the native OS stack.
Reactive PipelinesSpring WebFlux, Micronaut, Quarkus (Mutiny)Reactive Streams (Mono/Flux)Request stages form an event-driven DAG; execution is pushed through ring buffers and work-stealing pools.
Static CompositionRust (Axum, Tower), C++Compile-time nested decorator types (tower::Service)Flattened into a single state machine enum; polled iteratively on the event loop with no recursion.

The Complete Catalog: Seven (7) Implementation Styles in Java

1. Classic GoF (Self-Linked Pointers)

Each handler stores a direct reference to the next concrete handler in a singly linked list structure:

public abstract class BaseHandler {
    private BaseHandler next;

    public BaseHandler linkWith(BaseHandler next) {
        this.next = next;
        return next; // Enables fluent chaining: h1.linkWith(h2).linkWith(h3)
    }

    public void handle(Context ctx) {
        if (process(ctx) && next != null) {
            next.handle(ctx);
        }
    }

    // Return false to short-circuit the chain
    protected abstract boolean process(Context ctx);
}

2. Centralized Coordinator (Servlet / Tomcat Style)

Handlers do not know about each other. A dedicated Chain coordinator maintains an internal list and an index pointer, passing itself into each handler to allow mutual recursion:

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Filter {
    void doFilter(Context ctx, FilterChain chain);
}

public class FilterChain {
    private final List<Filter> filters = new ArrayList<>();
    private int index = 0;

    public FilterChain addFilter(Filter filter) {
        filters.add(filter);
        return this;
    }

    public void doFilter(Context ctx) {
        if (index < filters.size()) {
            Filter filter = filters.get(index++);
            filter.doFilter(ctx, this);
        }
    }
}

3. Flat Iterative Loop (Stack-Safe Short-Circuiting)

A coordinator loops over an ordered collection using standard iterative control flow. Handlers return an execution status instead of delegating to a successor:

public enum StepResult { CONTINUE, STOP }

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Step {
    StepResult execute(Context ctx);
}

public class IterativePipeline {
    private final List<Step> steps = new ArrayList<>();

    public IterativePipeline addStep(Step step) {
        steps.add(step);
        return this;
    }

    public void run(Context ctx) {
        for (Step step : steps) {
            if (step.execute(ctx) == StepResult.STOP) {
                break; // Clean short-circuit
            }
        }
    }
}

4. Functional Composition (java.util.function)

Leverages standard functional interfaces to fold multiple operations into a single composite function:

// Option A: Validation Chains with Predicate
Predicate<Order> isNotNull = Objects::nonNull;
Predicate<Order> hasValidAmount = o -> o.getAmount() > 0;
Predicate<Order> hasValidAddress = o -> o.getAddress() != null;

// Short-circuiting pipeline using logical AND
Predicate<Order> orderValidator = isNotNull
    .and(hasValidAmount)
    .and(hasValidAddress);

boolean isValid = orderValidator.test(new Order());

// Option B: Transformation Pipelines with Function
Function<String, String> sanitize = raw -> raw.strip();
Function<String, String> mask = text -> text.replaceAll("(?i)password=\\w+", "password=***");
Function<String, String> truncate = text -> text.length() > 100 ? text.substring(0, 100) : text;

Function<String, String> pipeline = sanitize.andThen(mask).andThen(truncate);
String result = pipeline.apply("  password=secret123 data  ");

5. Decorator / Constructor Nesting ("Russian Doll")

Handlers wrap downstream handlers at instantiation time. Each handler implements the same core interface and delegates directly to an injected instance:

public interface RequestHandler {
    Response handle(Request req);
}

public class MetricsHandler implements RequestHandler {
    private final RequestHandler next;

    public MetricsHandler(RequestHandler next) {
        this.next = next;
    }

    @Override
    public Response handle(Request req) {
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        Response res = next.handle(req); // Delegate downward
        System.out.println("Elapsed ms: " + (System.currentTimeMillis() - start));
        return res;
    }
}

// Assembly:
RequestHandler pipeline = new MetricsHandler(new SecurityHandler(new RootEndpoint()));
Response res = pipeline.handle(new Request());

6. Asynchronous Non-Blocking (CompletableFuture)

Used for I/O-heavy operations (database queries, network requests) where a thread should not block while the chain progresses:

@FunctionalInterface
public interface AsyncHandler {
    CompletableFuture<Context> handle(Context ctx);
}

public class AsyncPipeline {
    private final List<AsyncHandler> handlers = new ArrayList<>();

    public AsyncPipeline add(AsyncHandler handler) {
        handlers.add(handler);
        return this;
    }

    public CompletableFuture<Context> execute(Context initial) {
        CompletableFuture<Context> future = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(initial);
        for (AsyncHandler handler : handlers) {
            future = future.thenCompose(handler::handle);
        }
        return future;
    }
}

7. Spring Dependency Injection with @Order

In enterprise Spring applications, handlers are declared as Spring beans. Spring automatically collects and sorts them into an injected List based on precedence:

public interface OrderValidationStep {
    void validate(Order order);
}

@Component
@Order(1)
public class InventoryCheckStep implements OrderValidationStep {
    public void validate(Order order) { /* check stock */ }
}

@Component
@Order(2)
public class PaymentAuthorizationStep implements OrderValidationStep {
    public void validate(Order order) { /* check credit */ }
}

@Service
public class OrderProcessingService {
    // Spring injects all beans implementing OrderValidationStep in @Order sequence
    private final List<OrderValidationStep> validationSteps;

    public OrderProcessingService(List<OrderValidationStep> validationSteps) {
        this.validationSteps = validationSteps;
    }

    public void processOrder(Order order) {
        for (OrderValidationStep step : validationSteps) {
            step.validate(order); // Iterative execution
        }
    }
}

Comparison of Implementation Styles

Implementation StyleStack Memory"Around" Logic?Flow ControlPrimary Use Case
1. Classic GoF$O(N)$ RecursionDifficultNext pointerSimple, self-contained educational implementations
2. Centralized Coordinator$O(N)$ RecursionNativeIndex pointerWeb middleware, Servlets, Spring Security
3. Flat Iterative Loop$O(1)$ FlatNobreak / enumValidation engines, rule checks, short-circuit processing
4. Functional Composition$O(N)$ ClosuresNoBuilt-in short-circuitData sanitization, payload transformation, boolean checks
5. Decorator Nesting$O(N)$ RecursionNativeDirect delegationStatic HTTP clients, stream wrappers, middleware
6. Asynchronous Pipeline$O(1)$ Stack (Heap)Via future hooksNon-blocking composeHigh-throughput network services, reactive apps
7. Spring @Order Injection$O(1)$ FlatVia custom runnerDependency InjectionEnterprise plug-and-play workflows, plugin systems

5. State Pattern

The State pattern allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object will appear to change its class.

Unlike an unwieldy state machine driven by giant switch (state) statements across every method, the State pattern encapsulates each state as an independent class implementing a state interface.

Technical Invariants

  1. State Polymorphism: State-specific logic is partitioned across subclasses. Adding a new state requires only adding a new state class without mutating existing ones.
  2. Context Delegation: The Context holds a reference to the CurrentState object and delegates actions to it: state.handleAction(context).
// State interface
public interface OrderState {
    void pay(OrderContext ctx);
    void ship(OrderContext ctx);
    void cancel(OrderContext ctx);
}

// Context
public class OrderContext {
    private OrderState state = new PendingPaymentState();

    public void setState(OrderState state) { this.state = state; }

    public void pay() { state.pay(this); }
    public void ship() { state.ship(this); }
    public void cancel() { state.cancel(this); }
}

// Concrete State: Pending Payment
public class PendingPaymentState implements OrderState {
    @Override
    public void pay(OrderContext ctx) {
        System.out.println("Payment processed successfully.");
        ctx.setState(new PaidState());
    }

    @Override
    public void ship(OrderContext ctx) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot ship an unpaid order!");
    }

    @Override
    public void cancel(OrderContext ctx) {
        System.out.println("Order cancelled.");
        ctx.setState(new CancelledState());
    }
}

// Concrete State: Paid
public class PaidState implements OrderState {
    @Override
    public void pay(OrderContext ctx) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Order is already paid.");
    }

    @Override
    public void ship(OrderContext ctx) {
        System.out.println("Dispatching parcel via courier.");
        ctx.setState(new ShippedState());
    }

    @Override
    public void cancel(OrderContext ctx) {
        System.out.println("Refunding money and cancelling order.");
        ctx.setState(new CancelledState());
    }
}

6. Template Method Pattern

The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in an operation, deferring some steps to subclasses. It lets subclasses redefine certain steps of an algorithm without changing the algorithm's overarching structure.

It exemplifies the "Hollywood Principle": Don't call us, we'll call you.

Technical Invariants

  1. Final Algorithm Skeleton: The base class provides a final template method dictating the invariant order of operations.
  2. Hook and Abstract Primitive Methods: Subclasses provide concrete implementations for abstract steps or selectively override optional hook methods.
public abstract class DataPipeline {

    // The Template Method (sealed algorithm execution order)
    public final void runPipeline() {
        readSource();
        parseData();
        if (requiresValidation()) {
            validate();
        }
        writeOutput();
    }

    protected abstract void readSource();
    protected abstract void parseData();
    protected abstract void writeOutput();

    // Hook method with default implementation
    protected boolean requiresValidation() {
        return true;
    }

    protected void validate() {
        System.out.println("Running standard schema validation.");
    }
}

// Subclass providing specific data formats
public class CsvDataPipeline extends DataPipeline {
    @Override
    protected void readSource() { System.out.println("Reading local CSV file."); }

    @Override
    protected void parseData() { System.out.println("Parsing comma-separated rows."); }

    @Override
    protected void writeOutput() { System.out.println("Ingesting records into PostgreSQL."); }
}

Real-World Occurrences

  • HttpServlet methods (service() calls doGet(), doPost()).
  • Testing framework runners (JUnit lifecycle methods).

7. Iterator Pattern

The Iterator pattern provides a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying internal representation (whether array, binary tree, hash table, or graph).

Technical Invariants

  1. Separation of Traversal from Storage: The aggregate class focuses solely on storing data; the iterator encapsulates current index/node tracking, traversal direction, and bounds checking.
  2. Concurrent Iteration: Multiple iterators can traverse the same collection independently at the same time.
public interface SimpleIterator<T> {
    boolean hasNext();
    T next();
}

public class BinaryTreeNode<T> {
    public T value;
    public BinaryTreeNode<T> left;
    public BinaryTreeNode<T> right;
}

// In-order traversal iterator for binary tree
public class InOrderTreeIterator<T> implements SimpleIterator<T> {
    private final Deque<BinaryTreeNode<T>> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public InOrderTreeIterator(BinaryTreeNode<T> root) {
        pushLeft(root);
    }

    private void pushLeft(BinaryTreeNode<T> node) {
        while (node != null) {
            stack.push(node);
            node = node.left;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public boolean hasNext() {
        return !stack.isEmpty();
    }

    @Override
    public T next() {
        if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        BinaryTreeNode<T> node = stack.pop();
        pushLeft(node.right);
        return node.value;
    }
}

8. Mediator Pattern

The Mediator pattern defines an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact. It promotes loose coupling by keeping objects from referring to each other explicitly, allowing their interaction to be varied independently.

Instead of a chaotic web of many-to-many dependencies ($O(N^2)$ connections), all components communicate exclusively through the Mediator ($O(N)$ connections).

Direct Coupling (Chaotic):            Mediator Pattern (Star Hub):
   [Component A] ─── [Component B]       [Component A]     [Component B]
         │      ╳         │                    │                 │
         │    ╱   ╲       │                    ▼                 ▼
   [Component C] ─── [Component D]          [   Central Mediator   ]
                                               ▲                 ▲
                                               │                 │
                                         [Component C]     [Component D]

When building a central coordinator in real-world systems, implementations generally fall into four distinct architectural styles. Each style represents a different trade-off between traceability (how easily you can follow the execution path in an IDE) and extensibility (how easily you can add new components without modifying the coordinator).

1. The Explicit Orchestrator (Hardwired / Direct)

The mediator holds direct, typed references to every colleague. When an event occurs, colleagues call explicit methods on the mediator, and the mediator directly calls methods on other colleagues.

public class OrderCheckoutCoordinator {
    private final Cart cart;
    private final PaymentProcessor payment;
    private final InventoryClient inventory;
    private final EmailNotifier notifier;

    public OrderCheckoutCoordinator(Cart cart, PaymentProcessor payment, 
                                    InventoryClient inventory, EmailNotifier notifier) {
        this.cart = cart;
        this.payment = payment;
        this.inventory = inventory;
        this.notifier = notifier;
    }

    public void onUserClickCheckout(String userId) {
        List<Item> items = cart.getItems(userId);
        
        // Explicit sequential orchestration
        inventory.reserve(items);
        try {
            payment.charge(userId, cart.getTotal(userId));
            cart.clear(userId);
            notifier.sendSuccess(userId);
        } catch (PaymentFailedException e) {
            inventory.release(items); // Explicit compensating action
            notifier.sendFailure(userId, e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
  • How communication works: Direct method invocation (A -> Coordinator -> B).
  • Traceability: Maximum. You can set a breakpoint or use "Find Usages" / "Go to Implementation" in your IDE and trace every step without jumping through registries or reflections.
  • Failure Mode: Violates the Open/Closed Principle. Every time a new step is added (e.g., fraud check, loyalty points), this class grows larger and must be modified.

2. The Command Dispatcher (In-Process Bus / CQRS)

Instead of knowing every colleague, the mediator acts as a typed registry. Colleagues construct a self-contained Command/Query object and hand it to the mediator. The mediator matches the command type to its registered handler and executes it, often passing it through a pipeline of middleware (logging, validation, transactions).

// Generic Mediator Contract
public interface CommandBus {
    <R, C extends Command<R>> R execute(C command);
}

// Concrete Dispatcher using a registry
public class RegistryCommandBus implements CommandBus {
    private final Map<Class<? extends Command<?>>, CommandHandler<?, ?>> handlers = new HashMap<>();

    public <R, C extends Command<R>> void register(Class<C> commandClass, CommandHandler<C, R> handler) {
        handlers.put(commandClass, handler);
    }

    @Override
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public <R, C extends Command<R>> R execute(C command) {
        CommandHandler<C, R> handler = (CommandHandler<C, R>) handlers.get(command.getClass());
        if (handler == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("No handler registered for " + command.getClass());
        }
        return handler.handle(command);
    }
}

Usage at the caller site:

public class CheckoutController {
    private final CommandBus bus; // Controller only knows the bus

    public CheckoutController(CommandBus bus) {
        this.bus = bus;
    }

    public void checkout(String cartId) {
        // Submits command; bus finds ProcessPaymentHandler internally
        PaymentResult result = bus.execute(new ProcessPaymentCommand(cartId));
    }
}
  • How communication works: 1-to-1 dispatch via class type mapping.
  • Traceability: Medium. You cannot immediately jump to the handling logic with a direct method click; you must search for the handler implementing CommandHandler<YourCommand, ?>.
  • Where it shines: Modular monoliths and CQRS backends. Adding a new feature means adding a new Command and a new Handler class without touching existing service definitions or constructor signatures.

3. The Reactive / Event-Driven Hub (Pub/Sub)

Colleagues do not request actions; they publish domain events indicating that something has already happened. The mediator maintains subscriber lists and fans out notifications to interested listeners.

public class EventMediator {
    private final Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<Object>>> listeners = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public <T> void subscribe(Class<T> eventType, Consumer<T> listener) {
        listeners.computeIfAbsent(eventType, k -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>())
                 .add(obj -> listener.accept(eventType.cast(obj)));
    }

    public void publish(Object event) {
        List<Consumer<Object>> consumers = listeners.get(event.getClass());
        if (consumers != null) {
            for (Consumer<Object> consumer : consumers) {
                consumer.accept(event);
            }
        }
    }
}

Colleagues wire into the hub independently:

public class InventoryListener {
    public InventoryListener(EventMediator mediator) {
        mediator.subscribe(OrderPlacedEvent.class, this::onOrderPlaced);
    }

    private void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        // Deduct inventory independently
    }
}
  • How communication works: 1-to-Many broadcast (A -> Mediator -> [B, C, D]).
  • Traceability: Low. Control flow becomes implicit. If an event causes a secondary event, debugging can degenerate into tracing an "event cascade."
  • Where it shines: UI component frameworks (Swing/JavaFX listeners, document editors) and loosely-coupled domain integrations where publisher components should never care who is listening.

4. The State-Machine / Phase Coordinator

This variation is designed specifically to prevent race conditions across concurrent or multi-stage processes (e.g., distributed consensus, phased cluster rebalances, or complex multi-step wizards). The mediator does not just pass messages; it strictly owns the lifecycle phase and restricts what colleagues can do based on the current state.

public class RebalanceCoordinator {
    public enum Phase { STABLE, PREPARING_REBALANCE, REVOKING, ASSIGNING }

    private Phase currentPhase = Phase.STABLE;
    private final SubscriptionState subscriptions;
    private final NetworkFetcher fetcher;

    public synchronized void transitionTo(Phase targetPhase) {
        // Validates legal state transitions to prevent illegal interleaving
        if (!isValidTransition(this.currentPhase, targetPhase)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot move from " + currentPhase + " to " + targetPhase);
        }

        this.currentPhase = targetPhase;

        switch (targetPhase) {
            case REVOKING -> {
                fetcher.pauseFetches();
                fetcher.clearLocalBuffers();
                subscriptions.revokeAll();
            }
            case ASSIGNING -> {
                subscriptions.assignNewPartitions();
                fetcher.resumeFetches();
            }
            case STABLE -> {
                // Resume normal polling
            }
        }
    }

    private boolean isValidTransition(Phase from, Phase to) {
        return (from == Phase.STABLE && to == Phase.PREPARING_REBALANCE)
            || (from == Phase.PREPARING_REBALANCE && to == Phase.REVOKING)
            || (from == Phase.REVOKING && to == Phase.ASSIGNING)
            || (from == Phase.ASSIGNING && to == Phase.STABLE);
    }
}
  • How communication works: Colleagues signal condition changes, but the coordinator enforces lock-ordering and legal phase transitions before instructing colleagues to act.
  • Traceability: High. The state machine defines all valid system permutations in one place.
  • Where it shines: Low-level distributed clients (Kafka, Zookeeper, Raft clusters), transactional batch jobs, and workflow orchestrators.

Summary of Styles

StyleCommunication ModelDependency BindingPrimary StrengthPrimary Weakness
Explicit OrchestratorDirect CallsCompile-time concrete/interfaceZero indirection; straightforward debuggingHigh coupling to all colleagues; coordinator becomes large
Command Dispatcher1:1 Request/ResponseRuntime registry lookupSingle Responsibility; easily wrapped with middlewareHeavy class explosion (1 class per command)
Event-Driven Hub1:N Publish/SubscribeDynamic listenersNear-zero coupling between publishers and subscribersHard to reason about execution order and event cascades
State CoordinatorPhased Lifecycle ControlState machine transitionsEnforces concurrency safety and valid system statesOverhead of state transition boilerplate

9. Memento Pattern

The Memento pattern captures and externalizes an object's internal state without violating encapsulation, allowing the object to be restored to this state later.

Technical Invariants

  1. Three Distinct Roles:
    • Originator: The domain object that produces a snapshot of its state and can rehydrate itself from a memento.
    • Memento: The passive value object holding the serialized snapshot. Its internal state should be opaque or read-only to outside objects.
    • Caretaker: Responsible for the memento's safekeeping (e.g., an undo stack or disk storage), but never inspects or modifies the memento's contents.
// Memento (Immutable snapshot)
public record CanvasMemento(String jsonLayersState, long timestamp) {}

// Originator
public class Canvas {
    private String layersState;

    public void setLayersState(String state) { this.layersState = state; }
    public String getLayersState() { return layersState; }

    public CanvasMemento save() {
        return new CanvasMemento(layersState, System.currentTimeMillis());
    }

    public void restore(CanvasMemento memento) {
        this.layersState = memento.jsonLayersState();
    }
}

// Caretaker
public class CanvasHistory {
    private final Deque<CanvasMemento> history = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void push(CanvasMemento memento) { history.push(memento); }
    public CanvasMemento pop() { return history.pop(); }
}

10. Visitor Pattern

The Visitor pattern lets you define a new operation on an object structure without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates.

It implements Double Dispatch: the operation that gets executed depends on both the runtime type of the Visitor and the runtime type of the Visited Element.

Technical Invariants

  1. Element Interface: Declares accept(Visitor visitor).
  2. Double Dispatch Resolution: Inside the element, it calls visitor.visit(this), passing its concrete self so the compiler selects the correctly overloaded method.
// Element hierarchy
public interface AstNode {
    void accept(AstVisitor visitor);
}

public class VariableNode implements AstNode {
    public final String name;
    public VariableNode(String name) { this.name = name; }

    @Override
    public void accept(AstVisitor visitor) {
        visitor.visit(this); // Double dispatch!
    }
}

public class BinaryOpNode implements AstNode {
    public final AstNode left;
    public final AstNode right;
    public final String operator;

    public BinaryOpNode(AstNode left, String operator, AstNode right) {
        this.left = left;
        this.operator = operator;
        this.right = right;
    }

    @Override
    public void accept(AstVisitor visitor) {
        visitor.visit(this);
    }
}

// Visitor Interface
public interface AstVisitor {
    void visit(VariableNode node);
    void visit(BinaryOpNode node);
}

// Concrete Visitor: Pretty Printer
public class PrettyPrintVisitor implements AstVisitor {
    @Override
    public void visit(VariableNode node) {
        System.out.print(node.name);
    }

    @Override
    public void visit(BinaryOpNode node) {
        System.out.print("(");
        node.left.accept(this);
        System.out.print(" " + node.operator + " ");
        node.right.accept(this);
        System.out.print(")");
    }
}

Behavioral Patterns Decision Matrix

When You Want To...Recommended Pattern
Swap algorithms or business calculations dynamically at runtimeStrategy
Broadcast state changes to multiple unknown consumersObserver
Queue operations, execute asynchronously, or support multi-level undoCommand
Pass requests through an ordered series of handlers/filtersChain of Responsibility
Change an object's behavior based on internal state transitionsState
Enforce an algorithm's overall skeleton while allowing sub-step customizationsTemplate Method
Traverse complex data structures without exposing internal node layoutsIterator
Disentangle dense $M \times N$ object interactions through a single coordinatorMediator
Take checkpoints/snapshots of internal state without breaking encapsulationMemento
Add new analyses/transformations to a fixed class hierarchy without modifying itVisitor
